name: Habits
problem: A small habit tracker for one person. I want to define a few daily habits, tick them off each day, and see streaks and a calendar of the last months. It runs locally in the browser and works offline.
aspects: Ticking a habit must take one tap and feel instant
Streaks must be correct across months, leap years and time zones
Data must never be lost when the page reloads
constraints: TypeScript, Vite, no UI framework heavier than Preact
Data stays in the browser (IndexedDB), no backend
Unit tests for the streak and calendar logic

outcome.summary_plain: You get a working habit tracker that runs in your browser with no server. You can add your own habits with a name and a colour, tick them off for today with one tap, and go back and fix any of the last seven days. Each habit shows its current and longest streak and a heatmap of the last six months. Everything is saved in the browser, so closing the tab or reloading keeps your data, and you can download it all as a JSON file and load it back later.

you_will_see.what: Today's date, a progress bar with 'x of N done', and one large row per habit: a coloured circle to tap, the name, a seven-day strip and the current and longest streak
The seven-day strip is tappable: each of the last seven days can be ticked or unticked straight from the row
A row of day chips for the last seven days (yesterday selected by default) and the habit list for whichever day you pick, so you can fix a missed day on the phone too
A six-month heatmap for the habit you select, with a missed/done legend
Working buttons: New habit, Reorder, Export JSON and Import
Set the name and pick a colour; rename, recolour or archive an existing habit (archived habits leave the list but keep their history)
Move habits up and down; the order sticks after a reload
Reloading the page keeps every habit and every tick; the app also opens with no internet connection after the first visit

stays_the_same: The look and the layout are the one you agreed on in sketch v1 (Today list): same dark theme, same colours, same row and card design, same order of the blocks down the page
Still one screen; the tab switcher used in the sketch to compare three directions is gone
The six-month heatmap stays a read-only picture — you cannot tick a day by clicking it there
Still local-only: no account, no sync, no backend, nothing leaves your browser
to_see_it: Run `cd web && npm install && npm run dev` and open the address it prints (http://localhost:5173)

open_questions.question: How far back should you be able to tick a day?
open_questions.proposed_answer: The last seven days, through the row strip and the catch-up day chips; older days stay visible in the heatmap but read-only
open_questions.why_it_matters: Editing arbitrary history means a date picker and tap targets on the nine-pixel heatmap cells, which is a different screen

open_questions.question: The sketch's catch-up block was fixed to 'Yesterday'. Turning it into a seven-day chooser adds a row of day chips above that card. Good?
open_questions.proposed_answer: Yes — same card in the same place, with a small row of day chips on top, yesterday selected by default; without it there is no way to fix a past day on a phone, where the seven-day strip is hidden
open_questions.why_it_matters: It is the one visible addition to the agreed layout

open_questions.question: How do you pick which habit the bottom heatmap shows? In the sketch it was always the first one.
open_questions.proposed_answer: Tapping the habit's name selects it for the heatmap (the coloured circle stays a pure one-tap tick); the selected habit is remembered across reloads
open_questions.why_it_matters: The row has several tap targets, so the split has to be decided before the row is built

open_questions.question: When you import a JSON file, should it replace everything or merge with what is there?
open_questions.proposed_answer: Replace everything, after a confirmation dialog that says so
open_questions.why_it_matters: Merging needs conflict rules for habits with the same name, which is a lot more work

outcome.overview: Addressed: the brief does ask for past days, so rather than trimming the promise I extended `p1-today-screen` to actually build a full week of catch-up — the 7-day spark cells become tap targets on desktop, and the catch-up block gains a day-chip selector (defaulting to yesterday) so the same editing works at 375 px, where the spark is hidden. Acceptance criteria now check both paths, and the heatmap staying read-only is recorded as an open question.

scope.reason: A new single-screen browser app: persistence, one screen, habit management, export/import and unit tests. The owner already picked the layout in sketch v1, and there is no existing system or data to break.

process.why: Medium job (M, low risk): at most 3 phases, each reviewed.

handoff.summary_plain: The app now works exactly as scoped: you can add/rename/recolour/reorder/archive habits, tick today or any of the last 7 days with one tap, see correct current/longest streaks, and view a 6-month heatmap per habit. Everything is saved to IndexedDB (survives reload), and you can export/import your data as JSON. The app also now installs and works with no internet connection. The look matches the agreed sketch (dark theme, same cards/rows, tab switcher removed, heatmap stays read-only). The only nuance: on a phone-width screen the 7-day tick strip on each row is hidden by design — fixing a past day there goes through the 'Catch up' block instead, which is why that block exists as a 7-day chooser.

delivered.promise: Habits: create, rename, reorder, archive, name + colour
delivered.note: HabitDialog + reorder buttons + Archived panel, all wired to IndexedDB.

delivered.promise: Daily check-in: one tap today, editable for the last 7 days
delivered.note: Optimistic UI update, then async write; rollback on failure.

delivered.promise: Streaks: current and longest per habit
delivered.note: Heavily unit-tested across leap years, month/year boundaries, and DST in two time zones.

delivered.promise: Calendar: 6-month heatmap per habit, read-only
delivered.note: Heatmap cells are plain divs, not clickable, as agreed.

delivered.promise: Export to JSON / import back with replace-all confirmation
delivered.note: Import shows a confirm dialog stating it replaces all current data; malformed files are rejected with a clear message.

delivered.promise: Data never lost on reload
delivered.note: All state loads from IndexedDB on mount; selected habit for the heatmap also persists via localStorage.

delivered.promise: Works offline after first visit
delivered.note: vite-plugin-pwa generates a service worker + manifest; verified with a real offline browser reload in the task notes.

delivered.promise: Same look/layout as agreed sketch v1 (Today list), tab switcher removed, still one screen, still local-only
delivered.note: styles.css was copied byte-for-byte from the sketch; no `.switch` element remains.

delivered.promise: Seven-day strip tappable directly on each habit row
delivered.note: Works on desktop/tablet widths; CSS hides this strip on phone-width screens (≤560px), where only the Catch-up block below can fix a past day.

how_to_see: cd web && npm install (if not already done)
npm run dev — opens the app at the printed localhost URL (normally http://localhost:5173)
Tick a habit, reload the page, confirm the tick survived
Try New habit / Reorder / Export JSON / Import from the bottom bar
To check offline support specifically: npm run build && npm run preview, load the page once, then disconnect from the internet and reload — the app and your data should still appear
known_gaps: On phone-width screens the 7-day tick strip on each habit row is hidden by CSS; past-day edits there go through the Catch-up block instead (by design, but visually different from the desktop screenshot).
No 'new version available' prompt when the app updates itself offline — updates apply silently in the background (explicitly called out as in-scope-as-is in the build notes).
All automated checks (install, typecheck, tests, build) passed on their most recent runs — nothing is currently failing.

name: Links
problem: A small personal URL shortener. I want to turn long URLs into short codes, share them, and see how many times each link was opened. Single user, runs on my own machine or a small VPS.
aspects: Codes must be unguessable enough that links are not trivially enumerable
Redirects must be fast and never break for existing codes
Everything must be covered by automated tests
constraints: SQLite for storage, no external database server

outcome.summary_plain: You get a small link shortener you run on your own machine or a VPS. You paste a long link into a page, optionally give it your own short name, and get back a short link you can share. Opening a short link sends the visitor straight to the original page and quietly counts the visit. The same page lists all your links with how many times each was opened and when it was last used.

you_will_see.what: The dark 'Tool' page: a one-row form with a long-link field, an optional name field and a Shorten button; below it two big counters for total links and total opens; then a table of code, target, opens, last open and copy.
A green confirmation line with the new short link after a successful shorten, and a red line with a readable reason when the address is not valid or the custom name is already taken.

you_will_see.where: A short link in any browser or with curl
you_will_see.what: An immediate redirect to the original address; the open count for that link goes up by one on the page.
A plain 'Not found' page instead of a redirect.
`npm test` runs the full test suite covering shortening, redirects, counting and validation, and exits cleanly.

stays_the_same: The look and layout are exactly the 'Tool' sketch you approved; nothing about the design is being reconsidered.
The light 'friendly' alternative design is removed, along with the /_alt address that served it during the sketch.
There is still no login: anyone who can reach the port can create links and see the list.
There is no way to delete or edit a link, and the list shows every link on one page without paging.
to_see_it: Run `npm install` once, then `npm start`, and open http://localhost:8080
Needs Node 24 or newer (your machine has 26.7)

open_questions.question: Your brief says Node 22+, but the built-in SQLite the sketch uses is only stable from Node 24 onwards. Require Node 24+, or add the better-sqlite3 package so Node 22 keeps working?
open_questions.proposed_answer: Require Node 24 or newer and record that in the project manifest. Your machine runs 26.7, and this keeps the promise of zero runtime dependencies.
open_questions.why_it_matters: The alternative adds a native dependency that has to be compiled on every machine you deploy to, which is the opposite of the 'minimal dependencies' constraint.

open_questions.question: If you put this on a VPS, should creating links and viewing the list require a secret, or is the whole thing open to anyone who finds the address?
open_questions.proposed_answer: Leave it open, as the sketch had it. Redirects must stay public in any case.
open_questions.why_it_matters: An open shortener on a public VPS lets strangers hide their own links behind your domain. Adding a secret later changes how you call it and how the page works.

outcome.overview: Two fields were over the length limits; shortened, everything else unchanged.

scope.reason: A new, empty repository: three small endpoints, one static page and a SQLite data layer, all shown working in the agreed sketch. Nothing existing changes, and the look is fixed by the sketch the owner picked.

process.why: Small, low-risk job (S): one phase, one review at the end.

handoff.summary_plain: The shortener works end-to-end: you can paste a URL on the dark 'Tool' page (matching the approved sketch exactly), optionally give it a custom name, get a short link back, and opening that link redirects immediately while the open count and 'last opened' time update on the page. Unknown codes show a plain 'Not found' page. Codes are cryptographically random and effectively unguessable. The light 'friendly' design and its /_alt route were removed as agreed, there's still no login, and no delete/edit/pagination was added — all as planned. The full automated test suite passes. The only thing not literally watched in a browser is the green/red confirmation message on the form, which was verified by reading the code and testing the API directly instead of a live screenshot.

delivered.promise: Shorten links: POST a URL, get a short code, optional custom alias, URL validation
delivered.note: Validates http/https only, alias pattern-checked and race-safe 409 on collision

delivered.promise: Redirect: GET /:code returns 302 to the original URL; 404 for unknown codes
delivered.note: Indexed lookup; click recording failure can't block the redirect (tested)

delivered.promise: Click stats: count opens with timestamp, endpoint listing links with counts
delivered.note: GET /api/links returns clicks + lastClickAt, computed in SQL

delivered.promise: Minimal web page: form + table of links with counts, matching the 'Tool' sketch
delivered.note: Screenshots compared directly against the approved sketch — layout matches, including mobile column drop

delivered.promise: Green success / red error message on the form
delivered.note: Verified by reading the submit handler and testing the API's error responses directly, not by watching it in a live browser

delivered.promise: Codes unguessable / not trivially enumerable
delivered.note: 7 chars from a 56-char alphabet via crypto.getRandomValues with rejection sampling; ~1.7 trillion combinations

delivered.promise: Light 'friendly' design and /_alt route removed
delivered.note: Confirmed absent from the codebase; a test asserts /_alt now 404s

delivered.promise: No login; open to anyone who reaches the port
delivered.note: No auth code anywhere in the server

delivered.promise: No delete/edit/pagination; links never expire
delivered.note: Confirmed absent, as intentionally decided before building

delivered.promise: Full automated test suite (npm test)
delivered.note: Recorded checks show npm test passing; covers shortening, redirects, counting, validation

delivered.promise: Node 24+ requirement recorded, zero runtime dependencies
delivered.note: package.json engines field set; only dev dependencies present

how_to_see: Run `npm install` then `npm start` in the project directory
Open http://localhost:8080 in a browser — shorten a URL, note the short link
Open the short link in a new tab, confirm it redirects, then reload the main page and see the open count and 'last open' time update
Try a bogus code like http://localhost:8080/zzzzzzz to see the 'Not found' page
Run `npm test` to see the full suite pass
known_gaps: The form's success/error message was verified by code reading and direct API calls, not a live screenshot, due to a headless-browser cross-origin limitation. Low risk; worth a 30-second manual check.

name: Recipe scaler
problem: A web page where I paste a recipe, pick how many servings I want, and get the ingredient amounts scaled, with sensible unit conversions (grams, cups, spoons).
aspects: Parsing must handle fractions like 1 1/2 and ranges like 2-3
Converted amounts must be rounded to what you can measure in a kitchen
